data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The rial's peg to the US dollar (since 1986) delivers low inflation: 12.6% in 2008 on the commodity boom was the outlier, with most years at 0-4% and mild deflation of -0.4% in 2020. The IMF projects 1.0% for 2025. The 2021 introduction of 5% VAT added only a one-off bump (1.7% inflation that year). The central bank follows the Fed; the peg has never been seriously tested, and price stability is well established.
debt_management: Oman went from negligible debt (7.6% of GDP in 2006, just 4.0% in 2014) to 67.9% in 2020 as the 2014-16 oil crash and COVID forced borrowing, including debut international bonds. Disciplined consolidation under Sultan Haitham, plus the 2022 windfall, cut it to a projected 35.8% in 2025. GDP swung from $42.6bn (2006) to $109.8bn (2022) with oil. Unlike Bahrain, Oman adjusted: VAT, subsidy reform, and spending restraint under the medium-term fiscal plan have put debt on a clearly declining path.

key_events.event: Arab Spring-inspired protests won handouts and jobs pledges, raising the wage bill.
Oil crash; debt surged from 4.0% to 29.3% as deficits opened.
Sultan Qaboos died in January; Haitham succeeded. COVID and the oil crash pushed debt to 67.9%.
Oil windfall; GDP hit $109.8bn and debt fell to 41.7%.
Vision 2040 diversification continued; debt projected at 35.8% in 2025.

outlook_next_decade: Oman is the Gulf's most credible fiscal turnaround story: debt is falling, buffers are being rebuilt, and Vision 2040 targets logistics, tourism, and manufacturing diversification. The base case is moderate growth with continued consolidation. Risks are oil-price dependence (still dominant), water scarcity, and whether diversification delivers jobs for a young population. Analytical assessment: the trajectory is favorable, but the next oil downturn will test whether reforms or backsliding prevail.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
